description: How coal went from king to underdog while solar and wind exploded — U.S. electricity generation by fuel (2006–2025).
youtube_description:
The U.S. Power Shift — how electricity generation in America remixed itself from 2006 to 2025.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro — The rise and fall in one chart
0:20 2006: Coal still dominates (coal ~2,083 TWh)
0:45 2008–2014: Fracking, cheap gas and the first cracks in coal
1:25 2015–2020: Renewables begin to climb; gas takes the crown
2:00 2020–2023: Pandemic dip, then a renewable surge (wind & solar boom)
2:45 2022: Policy inflection — IRA and big tax credits (renewables accelerate)
3:15 2023 snapshot: Coal ~873 TWh, Gas ~1,390 TWh, Wind ~380 TWh, Solar ~200.4 TWh
3:40 2024–2025 estimates and what to expect next
4:10 Closing notes & sources

What this shows: In 2006 coal supplied roughly 2,083 TWh of U.S. electricity. By 2023 coal had fallen below 900 TWh (873 TWh) while natural gas rose to become the largest single source (roughly 1,390 TWh in 2023). Wind and solar went from niche — wind ~61 TWh and solar ~0.7 TWh in 2006 — to major players: wind crossed the hundreds-of-TWh threshold in the 2010s and solar hit ~200.4 TWh in 2023. Our 2024–2025 numbers are reasonable industry projections based on EIA trendlines and policy impacts (marked in the video).

Sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) annual/net generation tables, SEIA solar deployment reports, IEA country datasets, EIA Electricity Monthly — specific yearly numbers pulled from EIA tables and consolidated for visualization. 2024–2025 are marked as estimates based on EIA short-term trends and policy-driven deployment rates.

instagram_caption:
⚡️ The chart that rewired America’s grid — and it’s not what your grandparents grew up with.

From 2006 to 2025 the U.S. electricity mix went through a cinematic reversal: coal led the pack in 2006 at about 2,083 TWh. By 2023 coal had collapsed to roughly 873 TWh — less than half its mid-2000s output. Natural gas went the other way: ~898 TWh in 2006 and surging past coal to hit ~1,390 TWh in 2023, with estimates of ~1,650 TWh by 2025 as gas continues to supply firm power.

The real story though is the renewables explosion. Wind climbed from ~61 TWh in 2006 to hundreds of TWh by the 2010s (wind hit ~380 TWh in 2021–2023 territory). Solar? Practically invisible in 2006 (~0.7 TWh) — and then exponential growth: ~200.4 TWh in 2023 and modelled near ~260 TWh by 2025. Why the leap? Cheap PV, state renewable mandates, federal incentives, and falling levelized costs turned rooftop and utility-scale solar into a mainstream source.

Key turning points: the shale gas boom (late 2000s–2010s) undercut coal economically; the 2010s saw rapid wind build-outs; the Inflation Reduction Act and tax credits in 2022 accelerated utility solar and storage deployments — you can see those inflection points in the data lines. Pandemic-related demand shocks in 2020 nudged generation mixes too, briefly lowering total generation and accelerating retirements.

Which line surprised you most — the collapse of coal, the grip of gas, or solar’s rocket? Drop a comment with the fuel you think will lead America in 2030 and why. Headline: The U.S. Power Shift — coal collapses while solar and wind explode (2006–2025).

Detailed: In 2006 coal produced roughly 2,083 TWh of electricity in the United States. By 2023 coal generation had fallen to about 873 TWh, a decline driven by cheap natural gas, pollution regulations, market competition from renewables, and plant retirements. Natural gas rose from ~898 TWh in 2006 to become the largest single source in the 2010s and early 2020s (roughly 1,390 TWh in 2023). Wind and solar swung from marginal players — wind ~61 TWh and solar ~0.7 TWh in 2006 — to central contributors: wind reached the hundreds of TWh, and solar hit ~200.4 TWh in 2023. Our timeline runs through 2025, with 2024–2025 values shown as reasonable industry projections.

Sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), SEIA, IEA.
